paragraphs: ABC-Bench evaluates whether language-model agents can carry out biological work that combines scientific knowledge with software skills. This matters because capabilities useful for discovery can also change biosecurity risks. The benchmark includes both benign and dual-use tasks, making it a measure of relevant agent capabilities rather than biological knowledge alone.

Its three task areas cover programming liquid-handling robots, designing DNA fragments for laboratory assembly, and evading DNA synthesis screening. These require agents to turn biological understanding into computational outputs. Across all three tasks, every tested agent exceeded the median expert human baseline. Performance was stronger where published knowledge and well-documented procedures were available, and weaker on a task requiring new bioinformatics reasoning.

The researchers also tested whether some generated outputs worked in a laboratory. In three experiments, scripts produced by o4-mini-high successfully directed an OpenTrons robot to assemble DNA with the expected sequences. These results connect benchmark performance to demonstrated laboratory execution, while the weaker novel-reasoning result distinguishes established-knowledge use from more original problem solving.
icml-2026-abc-bench-an-agentic-bio-capab.tldr: ABC-Bench finds that tested agents exceed median expert baselines on three biosecurity-relevant tasks, with selected robot-control outputs validated in the laboratory.

paragraphs: BioProBench addresses a gap between understanding biological text and reasoning accurately about experimental procedures. Autonomous experimentation requires models to handle procedural logic, quantities, and safety considerations. A model that understands a protocol broadly may still struggle with the precise reasoning needed to use it reliably.

The resource starts with BioProCorpus, a collection of 27,000 human-written protocols. From these documents, the researchers construct more than 550,000 task instances. The resulting dataset serves two purposes: supplying training material for biological procedural reasoning and providing a benchmark with new evaluation metrics. This connects the evaluation tasks to a substantial collection of existing human-authored procedures.

An evaluation of ten mainstream language models finds strong general comprehension but substantially weaker performance on deeper reasoning, numerical precision, and safety awareness. The researchers also introduce ProAgent, grounded in the corpus, and report a substantial advance over the previous state of the art. Together, these findings identify a specific capability gap and show that a corpus-grounded agent can improve performance on the benchmark.
icml-2026-bioprobench-a-corpus-and-bench.tldr: BioProBench exposes weaknesses in biological procedural reasoning and shows substantial gains from a corpus-grounded agent.

paragraphs: Faster Flash Decoding targets the cost of attention when language models generate text using long contexts. Selecting only relevant portions of the context can reduce work, but the selection process has its own costs. Existing strategies can require extra indexing information or spend substantial computation deciding what to retain.

The proposed framework combines selection and attention computation inside a single fused kernel. It scans content using low-bit quantization, avoiding external metadata indices, and reuses scanning results during computation. Its top-delta strategy dynamically filters blocks according to the attention distribution without requiring global synchronization. This joint hardware and algorithm design aims to make sparsity useful after accounting for the overhead of finding it.

FFD requires no additional training and is designed to plug into existing models. The reported results include up to an 11.6-fold kernel speedup at a context length of 256,000 and a 2.37-fold improvement in end-to-end throughput. Evaluations on Ruler and Longbench preserve model accuracy while using substantial sparsity. The distinct speed measurements show both local computational gains and their effect on overall generation throughput.
icml-2026-faster-than-flash-exploiting-a.tldr: FFD fuses sparse attention selection and computation to accelerate long-context decoding while maintaining accuracy in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Machine-learning interatomic potentials predict energies and forces for atomistic simulations. Good prediction errors alone can miss an important physical property: the energy surface should change smoothly as atomic configurations change. Artificial jumps, minima, or forces can therefore cause simulation problems even when conventional regression scores look favorable.

The paper introduces the Bond Smoothness Characterization Test, which probes predicted energy surfaces through controlled bond deformations. It checks configurations both close to equilibrium and farther away. The test detects several kinds of non-smooth behavior and correlates strongly with molecular-dynamics stability, while costing a fraction of the molecular-dynamics evaluation. This makes smoothness a practical signal for repeated model assessment.

The authors also use the test to guide architecture changes in an unconstrained Transformer. A differentiable nearest-neighbor algorithm and temperature-controlled attention reduce artifacts identified by the test. The resulting model combines low energy and force errors with stable molecular dynamics and robust atomistic property predictions. The contribution thus extends beyond scoring finished models: it provides feedback that can guide their design.
icml-2026-from-evaluation-to-design-usin.tldr: A low-cost bond-deformation test detects energy-surface artifacts and guides interatomic model changes that improve simulation behavior.

paragraphs: This paper studies hallucination detection for tasks that require reasoning. Existing detectors can perform well on question answering yet be less effective in this setting. The authors approach the problem using ideas from out-of-distribution detection, a field concerned with identifying inputs that differ from the distributions a model is equipped to handle.

The central connection is to treat next-token prediction as classification: the model chooses among possible tokens. That perspective creates a route for adapting detection techniques developed in areas such as computer vision. However, the transfer requires modifications that account for structural differences in language models. The contribution is therefore an adapted detection approach built around this classification view.

The resulting detectors require no training and operate from a single sample. The authors report strong hallucination-detection accuracy on reasoning tasks, supporting the usefulness of this reframing in a setting where existing approaches struggle. The findings present out-of-distribution detection as a promising, scalable direction for identifying unreliable outputs; the stated result concerns detection performance rather than eliminating hallucinations during generation.
icml-2026-from-out-of-distribution-detec.tldr: Adapting out-of-distribution detection to next-token prediction yields training-free hallucination detectors with strong reported accuracy on reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Midtraining mixes specialized examples with general pretraining data before a model enters posttraining. This paper proposes that the intermediate phase helps by bridging distributions: it gives posttraining a starting point closer to the data and tasks it will encounter. The explanation focuses on how training phases connect to one another.

Controlled pretraining experiments show the largest benefits in domains relatively distant from general pretraining data, including code and mathematics. Benefits grow with the proximity advantage that midtraining provides toward the target distribution. In these domains, mixed-data midtraining consistently beats continued training on specialized data alone, both on domain performance and on reducing forgetting.

A code-focused investigation finds that timing and mixture weight interact strongly. Earlier introduction accommodates larger specialized-data shares, whereas later introduction requires smaller ones. This suggests that increasing the specialized share late in training cannot compensate for missing a period of greater plasticity. More broadly, the authors suggest that similar bridging strategies may help transitions between other training phases, extending the proposed explanation beyond midtraining itself.
icml-2026-midtraining-bridges-pretrainin.tldr: Midtraining helps by bridging training distributions, with benefits shaped jointly by domain distance, introduction timing, and data mixture.

paragraphs: Next-Gen CAPTCHAs responds to the growing ability of agents to solve web challenges through graphical interfaces. The authors report that recent reasoning-heavy models reach pass rates as high as 90% on complex puzzles such as Bingo in earlier evaluations. This motivates challenges built around capabilities that still separate people from agents.

The proposed framework focuses on interactive perception, memory, decision-making, and action. Its dynamic tasks are designed to demand adaptive intuition rather than detailed advance planning. The underlying idea is to exploit a persistent human–agent cognitive gap through interactions that require users to respond as the task unfolds. The authors present this as a way to restore a useful distinction between human users and automated agents.

A generation pipeline supports scalable evaluation instead of relying on a fixed collection of challenges. For challenge types supported by the backend, the system can produce effectively unbounded instances. This qualification matters: the instance-generation claim applies to those supported types. The framework combines diverse interactive challenges with scalable generation as a proposed defense against increasingly capable GUI agents.
icml-2026-next-gen-captchas-leveraging-t.tldr: Next-Gen CAPTCHAs proposes scalable interactive challenges that exploit remaining differences between human and GUI-agent capabilities.

paragraphs: This paper examines tool-calling from two connected perspectives: whether evaluations measure it reliably and whether reinforcement learning teaches it efficiently. Tool use lets agents act beyond the knowledge stored in their parameters, making both the credibility of reported scores and the cost of training practically important.

The evaluation analysis finds that apparently minor implementation choices can substantially change results. These include random seeds, system prompts, the construction of multi-turn templates, and the way previous interactions or reasoning are retained. Sensitivity is especially pronounced in multi-turn settings. Without rigorous standardization, reported leaderboard positions can therefore reflect differences in evaluation setup as well as differences in model capability.

The training analysis identifies waste in two stages. During rollouts, many prompts provide no learning signal; during policy updates, optimization is computationally expensive. The authors introduce two techniques motivated by these observations and report substantial reductions in wall-clock training time without lower performance. Together, the findings connect better-controlled measurement with more efficient learning, addressing how tool-calling capability is both judged and acquired.
icml-2026-on-effectiveness-and-efficienc.tldr: Tool-calling scores depend strongly on evaluation details, while two proposed techniques accelerate reinforcement learning without reported performance loss.

paragraphs: PETS studies how to distribute a limited sampling budget across questions when answers are chosen by majority vote over stochastic reasoning attempts. Giving every question the same number of attempts can waste samples. The paper defines a self-consistency rate measuring agreement with the majority answer that an unlimited sampling budget would produce.

This definition turns allocation into an optimization problem. When all questions are available in advance, the authors connect reasoning traces to workers in crowdsourcing. That connection supplies theoretical tools and an efficient allocation algorithm based on majority voting. For questions arriving sequentially, they develop an online method that adjusts budgets to question difficulty while retaining theoretical guarantees and computational efficiency.

Experiments find that PETS consistently improves on uniform allocation. On GPQA, it achieves perfect self-consistency in both settings while reducing sampling budgets by up to 75% offline and 55% online. Here, perfect self-consistency means matching the infinite-budget majority vote, rather than necessarily answering every question correctly. The result shows that the chosen agreement target can be reached using substantially fewer samples.
icml-2026-pets-a-principled-framework-to.tldr: PETS allocates reasoning samples adaptively to match infinite-budget majority decisions more efficiently than uniform sampling.

paragraphs: Translation-equivalent prompts can produce inconsistent responses from the same language model. This paper treats that inconsistency as a property of response distributions across languages, giving multilingual reliability a formal optimization target. The goal is to make model behavior more consistent when a request retains its meaning through translation.

The authors define consistency through a bound on divergence between the original response distribution and its counterpart after a round trip across languages. They then propose penalized consistency optimization, which combines this divergence with a Kullback–Leibler penalty relative to a fixed reference model. The reference penalty constrains how far the optimized model moves while pursuing consistency.

Directly optimizing that objective requires expensive rollouts from the current policy. Direct consistency optimization provides a tractable surrogate that can instead be trained off-policy. Across multiple language models and 26 languages, it significantly improves consistency and outperforms existing methods. It also supports targeted alignment of low-resource languages. The contribution combines a formal definition with a more practical training procedure for improving the measured behavior.
icml-2026-post-training-language-models-.tldr: Direct consistency optimization improves agreement across translation-equivalent prompts using a tractable off-policy posttraining objective.

paragraphs: ProtDBench addresses a comparison problem in protein binder design: computational success metrics can mean different things under different evaluation protocols. The framework standardizes tasks, filtering procedures, and success criteria so that observed differences between design methods can be assessed under controlled conditions.

Using a large dataset annotated with wet-lab outcomes, the authors examine structure-prediction models used to verify candidate binders. They find substantial verifier-dependent bias and limited agreement even under identical filtering rules. This shows that the choice of evaluation model can materially influence which designs appear successful. The paper then evaluates representative open-source generative methods across ten diverse protein targets using a fixed protocol.

The framework also looks beyond success per generated sequence. It measures output within a fixed 24-hour budget and uses cluster-level success criteria to account for structural diversity. These views expose differences associated with filtering, success definitions, and computational throughput. ProtDBench makes the relationship between efficiency, success rate, and diversity more visible, supporting comparisons that reflect both candidate quality and the practical amount of useful output.
icml-2026-protdbench-a-unified-benchmark.tldr: ProtDBench standardizes protein binder evaluation and reveals how verifier choice, throughput, and diversity criteria alter apparent performance.

paragraphs: Generalist graph anomaly detection aims to identify unusual patterns in previously unseen graphs without retraining a detector for each graph. A central obstacle is that features from different domains can have different meanings. Making feature vectors the same size through projection does not necessarily align those meanings.

REFI-GAD addresses this issue with a shared relational fingerprint. It encodes anomaly-related information from both context and graph structure, giving the detector a common representation grounded in relationships. The intended benefit is semantic transfer: pretraining should teach cues that remain meaningful on new graphs, avoiding the negative transfer associated with inadequate alignment.

The model combines a transformer encoder for learning domain-invariant information with an SNR-guided refinement module for domain-specific adaptation. This separates the pursuit of shared knowledge from the need to respond to differences in a target graph. Across 14 datasets, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support relational fingerprints as a more useful foundation for transfer than alignment that only harmonizes feature dimensions.
icml-2026-rethinking-feature-alignment-i.tldr: REFI-GAD uses context-and-structure fingerprints to transfer anomaly-detection knowledge across graphs with heterogeneous features.

paragraphs: SAGE treats a language-model application as a complete inference pipeline, including retrieval, memory, refinement, generation, and tool use. When these stages are separate services, queues and resource interference can be difficult to understand across the whole application. That makes it harder to control the slowest requests and meet latency objectives.

The framework expresses pipelines as declarative dataflows and compiles them into distributed execution plans. Bounded queues apply backpressure so stages can regulate incoming work. Search, semantic state, memory, and refinement become operators with explicit resource and state contracts, helping locate the source of long delays. A unified control plane coordinates engines, batching, and admission across mixed workloads.

On 16 nodes, SAGE sustains 16 requests per second with more than 700 tokens per request and a median scheduling overhead of one millisecond. It reports 11.4-fold throughput scaling at 16 nodes, described as near-linear scale-out. Under contention between pipelines, it reduces P99 latency by 57% relative to simultaneous admission, demonstrating gains in the slow end of the request-latency distribution.
icml-2026-sage-a-dataflow-native-framewo.tldr: SAGE compiles complete LLM pipelines into coordinated distributed dataflows, improving throughput and tail latency in reported cluster tests.

paragraphs: BridgePolicy changes how diffusion-based robot policies use observations when generating actions. Existing approaches commonly give observations to the denoising network as conditions while starting the sampling process from random noise. The paper argues that this leaves perception and control less tightly connected than they could be.

The proposed policy embeds observations directly into the stochastic dynamics through a diffusion bridge. Sampling therefore begins from an informative prior shaped by what the robot observes. A technical obstacle is that diffusion bridges normally connect distributions with matching dimensionality, whereas images, robot states, and actions have different forms. A semantic aligner unifies visual and state inputs and aligns them with action representations.

This alignment makes the bridge formulation applicable to heterogeneous robot data. Across 52 simulation tasks from three benchmarks and five real-world tasks, BridgePolicy consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative policies. The reported results support the value of observation-informed sampling for control precision and reliability. The key methodological shift is where observations enter: they shape the sampling trajectory itself, as well as informing the generated behavior.
icml-2026-sample-from-what-you-see-visuo.tldr: BridgePolicy starts action generation from an observation-informed prior and reports stronger robot-control performance across simulated and real tasks.

paragraphs: SLASH examines why language models struggle with graph structure when graphs are presented as serialized text. The authors find evidence that models already reconstruct topology internally: their attention maps exhibit a sawtooth pattern aligned with a token-level representation of graph adjacency. This suggests that useful structural information exists inside the model.

The paper argues that an attention sink dilutes this information. Its theoretical account describes a representation bottleneck: the model's directional bias, useful for language processing, suppresses the local aggregation needed to reason over graph connections. The problem therefore involves how existing structural signals influence computation, as well as whether the model can represent those signals.

Structural Attention Sharpening redistributes attention to amplify the internal topology-aware behavior. It is training-free and designed as a plug-in intervention, avoiding the need to train an external graph adapter or fine-tune the model. Experiments on graph tasks and molecular prediction report significant, consistent improvements across diverse language models. These findings support attention redistribution as a way to make existing structural representations more useful for prediction.
icml-2026-slash-the-sink-sharpening-stru.tldr: SLASH redistributes attention without training to strengthen graph-structure signals already present inside language models.

paragraphs: Spiral RoPE studies how vision transformers encode the positions of image patches. Standard axial two-dimensional rotary embeddings handle horizontal and vertical coordinates separately. The authors identify this restriction to axis-aligned directions as an obstacle to representing oblique spatial relationships that occur naturally within images.

Their extension divides embedding channels into groups associated with uniformly distributed directions. For each group, a patch's position is projected onto the corresponding direction, and that projection determines the rotation. The resulting representation includes spatial relationships along multiple orientations. This directly changes the directional information available in the positional encoding while retaining a rotary construction.

Across classification, segmentation, and image-generation tasks, the authors report consistent performance improvements. Qualitative attention-map analysis also shows more concentrated activity on semantically relevant objects and better adherence to local object boundaries. These observations connect the numerical improvements to changes in where the models attend. Together, the findings support the importance of encoding spatial relationships beyond horizontal and vertical axes in vision transformers.
icml-2026-spiral-rope-rotate-your-rotary.tldr: Spiral RoPE encodes image positions along multiple directions, improving reported vision-task performance and object-focused attention.

paragraphs: SPARK addresses how to use language models' architectural knowledge when searching for better neural networks. Models can translate design ideas into executable code changes, but evaluating candidate architectures is expensive. Search therefore benefits when each proposed modification tests a focused idea and produces a more reliable change in behavior.

The paper identifies functional entanglement as a key obstacle. A code edit that appears local can alter several interacting functional factors, producing effects elsewhere in the network. SPARK explicitly selects the functional factor to change and conditions the edit on that choice. This gives the language model a more specific target for applying its architectural and coding knowledge.

The authors report that this procedure reduces entangled side effects and yields more targeted architecture modifications. On CLRS-DFS, SPARK achieves a 28.1-fold speedup in sample-efficient architecture evolution and a 22.9% relative improvement in out-of-distribution accuracy. These findings connect more controlled editing to both search efficiency and generalization. The reported speedup concerns sample-efficient evolution, so it describes how effectively evaluations advance the architecture search.
icml-2026-structured-progressive-knowled.tldr: SPARK makes LLM-guided architecture edits more targeted by selecting the functional factor to modify before generating the change.

paragraphs: TestExplora evaluates whether language models can discover software bugs before receiving reports about them. It distinguishes proactive discovery from preserving existing behavior and reproducing already-reported failures. Existing code may itself contain defects, so using that code as the sole reference can reward tests that merely confirm incorrect behavior.

The benchmark contains 2,389 tasks across 482 repositories and hides defect-related information. Models must compare implementation behavior with intent derived from documentation, which serves as the reference for judging correctness. A continuous, time-aware collection framework is also proposed to sustain the evaluation and reduce leakage risks associated with static datasets.

The model evaluation reaches a maximum Fail-to-Pass rate of 16.06%, showing substantial difficulty. A separate agentic configuration, SWEAgent with GPT-5-mini, achieves 17.27% F2P and 29.7% F2P@5. The analysis identifies cross-module interactions and agentic exploration as important factors in progress. These results suggest that repository exploration can improve proactive discovery, while the reported success rates show that the benchmark remains challenging even with an agentic setup.
icml-2026-testexplora-benchmarking-llms-.tldr: TestExplora measures bug discovery without defect clues and finds that proactive repository testing remains difficult, with gains from agentic exploration.

paragraphs: This paper examines why narrow-task fine-tuning can damage broader capabilities even when parameter changes appear small. Under fixed training conditions, the authors identify trajectory lock-in: task loss and broad generalization follow a shared, low-dimensional degradation curve. Many stabilizing methods mainly change how quickly training moves along that curve.

This produces a drift paradox. Two models can move comparable Euclidean distances in parameter space yet have different generalization outcomes. The authors introduce geometric probes that track the effective subspace of updates, along with an online harm signal. That signal reflects the extent to which curvature channels updates toward directions associated with broad degradation.

Within the studied narrow-adaptation settings, escaping lock-in requires a qualitative reorientation of the update subspace toward softer curvature modes, called a spectral bifurcation. This improves broad generalization while matching training performance. The authors validate the findings across model scales and modalities and report deployment procedures and overhead measurements. The central implication is that update direction and geometry reveal degradation patterns that magnitude-based stability proxies can miss.
icml-2026-the-geometry-of-narrow-fine-tu.tldr: Narrow fine-tuning can follow a shared degradation trajectory, with escape tied to reorienting update directions rather than merely limiting parameter drift.

paragraphs: Thoughtbubbles gives transformers a way to allocate extra computation internally during pretraining. Approaches based on explicit reasoning text rely on serially generated language. This method instead learns to expand or remove internal residual streams, allowing tokens that need more processing to receive parallel computation inside the network.

A token can form a bubble of cloned residual representations partway through the model. The decisions to fork or delete streams are learned using only the language-modeling loss. This makes adaptive computation part of ordinary pretraining, without requiring explicit reasoning-token supervision. The adaptation concerns how much internal processing different tokens receive.

Across model sizes from 150 million to 1.9 billion parameters, Thoughtbubbles outperforms standard decoder language models and non-adaptive parallel alternatives on perplexity and zero-shot evaluations while using half the training budget. It also achieves competitive GSM8K results with half the baseline token budget. These findings support learning adaptive internal computation early in training and motivate the authors' proposed direction of unifying training-time and inference-time scaling.
icml-2026-thoughtbubbles-an-unsupervised.tldr: Thoughtbubbles learns to fork and delete internal computation streams during pretraining, improving reported efficiency across several model sizes.

paragraphs: TimeLAVA assigns value to time-series data without training a predictive model. Standard valuation approaches can depend on a particular model or assume independent samples, overlooking temporal dependencies, patterns at different scales, and changing distributions. The paper instead evaluates how temporal segments contribute to reducing discrepancy from reference data.

Its discrepancy measure combines wavelet transforms with unbalanced optimal transport. Wavelets provide temporal localization at multiple scales, while the transport component supplies robustness to distributional shifts. Sensitivity analysis estimates segment contributions efficiently, and those values are aggregated into scores for individual time points. The reference comparison gives the valuation a defined distributional target.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees connecting these values to model-agnostic generalization and prove bounded sensitivity to outlier contamination. Experiments cover anomaly detection, data pruning, and label-noise detection on diverse real-world datasets. TimeLAVA produces significantly more informative scores than existing methods in those evaluations. The contribution is a valuation framework that accounts for temporal structure while avoiding the cost and model dependence of training a predictor to score the data.
icml-2026-timelava-learning-agnostic-val.tldr: TimeLAVA values temporal data through multiscale distributional comparisons, without model training, and reports improved scores for several data-curation tasks.

paragraphs: UniDrag connects fast aerodynamic prediction with vehicle-shape optimization. Given geometry, it predicts surface pressure, volume flow fields, drag coefficient, and a profile locating drag contributions along the vehicle. Its architecture combines enhanced Physics-Sliced Attention, expert routing, and modality-protected learning to prevent interference between the different prediction outputs.

At deployment, the trained surrogate stays frozen while gradients guide shape changes through Free-Form Deformation under engineering constraints. Expectation-over-Transformation is introduced to prevent optimization from exploiting weaknesses in the surrogate. This addresses a central risk of surrogate-based design: an apparently favorable prediction can result from model fragility rather than a physically better shape.

The researchers create a dataset of 15,000 geometries covering four vehicle body types using GPU-accelerated simulations. On this benchmark, UniDrag reports drag-coefficient prediction R-squared of 0.937, a stated 7.6% improvement over baselines. Shape optimization yields 13.7% mean CFD-verified drag reduction with a 100% success rate in the reported evaluation. Average displacement is 21.3 millimeters, or 0.46% of vehicle length, connecting the drag improvements to comparatively small geometry changes.
icml-2026-unidrag-unified-multi-field-pr.tldr: UniDrag combines aerodynamic prediction with constrained shape optimization, reporting CFD-verified drag reductions from small vehicle-geometry changes.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why language-model training losses can decrease slowly according to a power law. The authors identify a mechanism arising from two standard ingredients: softmax, which produces probabilities, and cross-entropy, which scores those probabilities against targets. Their claim concerns learning peaked distributions, including the next-token distributions relevant to language modeling.

Through systematic toy-model analysis and empirical evaluation of language models, they show that these ingredients can intrinsically produce power-law decay in both losses and gradients. As gradients diminish, optimization encounters a bottleneck. The analysis yields a loss-versus-time scaling exponent of one third, described as universal because it persists across many microscopic details within the studied setting.

The result supplies a mechanistic explanation for observed neural scaling behavior. It shows how slow convergence can emerge from the probability representation and training objective themselves when targets are peaked. That explanation suggests directions for improving training efficiency by reconsidering this mechanism. The paper presents those efficiency improvements as future possibilities arising from the analysis, rather than as a demonstrated replacement training method.
icml-2026-universal-one-third-time-scali.tldr: Softmax and cross-entropy can intrinsically produce one-third power-law loss scaling when learning peaked probability distributions.

paragraphs: WorldMirror unifies several forms of three-dimensional reconstruction in a single feed-forward model. It can accept geometric information such as camera poses, camera intrinsics, and depth maps alongside its inputs. This flexibility allows available prior knowledge to contribute to reconstruction instead of restricting the framework to image-only input or one specialized task.

The model jointly produces dense point clouds, depth maps across views, camera parameters, surface normals, and 3D Gaussians. These outputs represent complementary aspects of scene geometry and appearance. Producing them within one framework connects flexible geometric inputs with multiple prediction targets, allowing the same reconstruction system to support a broad collection of tasks.

The authors report gains from prior injection across all evaluated tasks, suggesting that input flexibility and joint prediction reinforce one another. WorldMirror achieves state-of-the-art results across benchmarks for cameras, point maps, depth, surface normals, and novel-view synthesis while retaining feed-forward inference efficiency. The findings support a unified approach in which available geometric knowledge improves several reconstruction outputs together, rather than helping only one narrowly defined prediction.
icml-2026-worldmirror-universal-3d-world.tldr: WorldMirror uses flexible geometric priors to improve multiple 3D reconstruction outputs within one efficient feed-forward model.

paragraphs: XYZFlow tackles the speed–quality trade-off in image generation. Diffusion models can produce strong images but need repeated sampling steps, while distilling them into few-step generators is difficult and depends heavily on teacher quality. The paper explores richer conditioning in flow matching as a route to efficient generation.

The authors interpret autoregressive modeling as implicitly straightening probability paths: more context reduces ambiguity about the trajectory toward an output. XYZFlow applies this idea along two dimensions. Temporal scaling conditions on the full denoising history. Spatial scaling uses Next Shortcut Prediction to generate patches sequentially, with previous patches' denoising trajectories serving as priors. Both supply additional structure to make the generation paths easier to identify and learn.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, competitive FID, and speedups of 7.2 to 8.5 times relative to the teacher. Next Shortcut Prediction also provides better quality–latency trade-offs than model scaling or reducing sampling steps in the reported comparisons. These results support richer temporal and spatial context as a useful way to improve efficient image generation.
icml-2026-xyzflow-scaling-multidimension.tldr: XYZFlow uses denoising history and preceding patch trajectories to improve image-generation speed and quality trade-offs.
